source.title: Etiquette in Society, in Business, in Politics and at Home
source.attribution: Emily Post, Etiquette in Society, in Business, in Politics and at Home, Project Gutenberg, public domain
source.notes: Public domain in the US. Emily Post died in 1960, so the book may still be in copyright in countries using life plus 70 years.

cards.title: Good manners are about how you treat people, not about money or status
cards.body:
Emily Post opens her famous book by knocking down an idea many readers expected her to defend: that good society means the rich and well born. Her real test was simpler. People earn their place by speaking well, being pleasant to be around, knowing the usual courtesies and, above all, paying instinctive attention to how others feel.

That is still the most useful way to think about etiquette. The rules about forks and invitations change with every generation, but the aim behind them stays the same. When you are unsure what the correct move is, ask which option would make the other person most comfortable. That answer is rarely wrong.
cards.quote: Best Society is not a fellowship of the wealthy, nor does it seek to exclude those who are not of exalted birth; but it is an association of gentle-folk
cards.apply_it: Next time you feel unsure about a social rule, ask yourself: what would make the other person feel most at ease?

quiz.question: According to Post, what really marks someone as well mannered?
options: Wealth and a good family name
Knowing every formal rule by heart
Instinctive consideration for the feelings of others
quiz.explanation: Post lists good speech, charm and social knowledge, but the heart of it is consideration for others' feelings.

cards.title: Never take more than your share, whether seats, road or food
cards.body:
Post says that consideration for the rights and feelings of others is the foundation that all social life is built on. She boils hundreds of rules down to one: never do anything that is unpleasant to others. Then she gives a very practical example of it. Don't take more than your share of the road, of chairs on a boat, of seats on a train or of food at the table.

The modern list writes itself: the bag on the empty train seat, the armrest hog, the double parking space, the person who takes the last three slices before others have had one. Before you spread out or help yourself, glance around and check whether there is enough to go round.
cards.quote: Never take more than your share--whether of the road in driving a car, of chairs on a boat or seats on a train, or food at the table.
cards.apply_it: On your next commute or shared meal, notice one moment where you could take a little less space or food so someone else has enough.

quiz.question: What does Post call the first rule of etiquette, which hundreds of others only explain?
options: Never do anything that is unpleasant to others
Always answer letters within a day
quiz.explanation: She says the first rule is never to do anything unpleasant to others, and taking more than your share is a clear example.

cards.title: Real manners are the same for the CEO and the cleaner
cards.body:
Post describes a well-bred man whose manners are the same whether he is in his dressing room or a ballroom, talking to a society hostess or to the laundress bringing in his clothes. Anyone whose good manners only appear in company, she says, is merely veneered.

This is one of the most reliable ways to read people today. Watch how someone treats a waiter, a receptionist or a junior colleague when they think nothing is at stake. Courtesy that switches on only for people who can help you is strategy, not manners. The goal is to be one person in every room, so that nobody you meet gets a cheaper version of you.
cards.quote: He whose manners are only put on in company is a veneered gentleman, not a real one.
cards.apply_it: Today, greet one person you usually overlook, such as a cleaner, driver or security guard, with the same warmth you would give your boss.

quiz.question: What does Post call someone whose manners only appear in company?
options: A veneered gentleman, not a real one
quiz.explanation: She says manners that are only put on in company are a veneer; real manners stay the same with everyone.

cards.title: How you treat people who serve you reveals your character
cards.body:
Post had no patience for the customer who snaps at a busy shop assistant for not dropping everyone else, then complains about her to the manager. Rudeness to anyone who serves you, she says, always shows poor upbringing and plain selfishness. She also notes that the people most anxious about their dignity are usually the ones who treat staff worst.

The same applies to call-centre agents, delivery drivers, baristas and hotel staff. They are often dealing with a queue, a system or a shortage they did not create. Patience costs you a few seconds and can change the whole day of the person in front of you.
cards.quote: Lack of consideration for those who in any capacity serve you, is always an evidence of ill-breeding, as well as of inexcusable selfishness.
cards.apply_it: The next time service is slow, say one kind sentence to the person serving you before you mention the problem.

quiz.question: According to Post, who tends to be rude to shop staff?
options: People who are insecure about their own dignity
quiz.explanation: She says it is the person afraid someone may encroach on her insecure dignity who shows no courtesy to staff.

cards.title: Keep your temper, because public outbursts jar everyone around you
cards.body:
Post treats self-control as central to good behaviour. Losing your temper, she says, hands the advantage to others. Showing anger, fear, hatred, embarrassment or wild hilarity in public is bad form, and she gives a refreshingly simple definition of bad form: anything that jars the feelings of the people around you.

This isn't a call to bottle everything up. It is a reminder that your strong feelings land on bystanders who did nothing to cause them. Shouting at a gate agent, ranting in a meeting or crying furious tears at a referee all make the room tense. Take the feeling somewhere private, calm down, and deal with the cause when you can speak steadily.
cards.quote: Exhibitions of anger, fear, hatred, embarrassment, ardor or hilarity, are all bad form in public. And bad form is merely an action which 'jars' the sensibilities of others.
cards.apply_it: Pick a phrase to use when anger rises in public, such as 'Give me a moment', and step away before you reply.

quiz.question: How does Post define 'bad form'?
options: An action that jars the sensibilities of others
Speaking to someone above your station
quiz.explanation: For Post, bad form is simply behaviour that jars on the people around you.

cards.title: Rescue the stranded guest, but don't force introductions on everyone
cards.body:
Post admits that knowing when to introduce people is one of the hardest social judgements. Her working rule is to introduce people whenever it bridges an awkward situation. She is equally hard on two kinds of host: the one who lets a guest stand alone and unknown in the middle of the room, and the one who drags reluctant people into meeting each other everywhere.

At a party, a new job or a school gate, watch for the person hovering at the edge with nobody to talk to. One introduction with a hook, such as 'Sam just moved here from Leeds', can change their whole evening. But you don't need to introduce everyone to everyone. Read the room.
cards.quote: The hostess who allows a guest to stand, awkward and unknown, in the middle of her drawing-room is no worse than she who pounces on every chance acquaintance and drags unwilling victims into forced recognition of each other
cards.apply_it: At your next gathering, find one person standing alone and introduce them to someone, adding one detail they might share.

quiz.question: What two hosting mistakes does Post put side by side?
options: Serving too much food and too little drink
Inviting too many people and too few
Leaving a guest stranded alone, and forcing introductions on everyone
quiz.explanation: She says the host who leaves a guest awkward and alone is no worse than the one who forces unwanted introductions.

cards.title: Shake hands briefly and warmly, and look the person in the face
cards.body:
Post observes that a handshake can create liking or irritation between two strangers in a second. She describes the limp hand offered like seaweed, the arm pumped sideways as if cleaning the air, and the crushing grip that grinds rings into fingers. All of them put people off.

Her recipe is short. Keep it brief, put some strength and warmth into the clasp, and look at the person while you do it. That still works, and the same spirit applies to whatever greeting is customary where you are, whether a nod, a bow or a wave on a video call: brief, warm and with real eye contact.
cards.quote: The proper handshake is made briefly; but there should be a feeling of strength and warmth in the clasp, and, as in bowing, one should at the same time look into the countenance of the person whose hand one takes.
cards.apply_it: Notice your next greeting: is it brief, warm, and are you looking at the person rather than past them?

quiz.question: Which handshake does Post recommend?
options: A brief clasp with strength and warmth, while looking at the person
A soft, relaxed touch with no grip
A crushing grip to show confidence
quiz.explanation: She wants it brief, warm and firm, with your eyes on the other person.

cards.title: When you've forgotten someone, don't announce it
cards.body:
Post deals with a moment everyone dreads: someone greets you and asks, 'You don't remember me, do you?' Her advice is to answer warmly, keep the chat going with neutral remarks, and quietly find out later who it was. Bluntly saying 'I don't remember you' is, in her words, rude and stupid. She adds that if a new acquaintance keeps getting your name wrong, you can let it pass once, then correct them simply.

The kindness here is in sparing the other person embarrassment. A modern version is a friendly 'Remind me where we met?' which is honest without being cold. And if someone keeps mangling your name, a light, matter-of-fact correction is perfectly polite.
cards.quote: your hiding the fact of your forgetfulness saves you from the rather rude and stupid situation of blankly declaring: 'I don't remember you.'
cards.locator: =The Retort Courteous to One You Have Forgotten= ¶1
cards.apply_it: Prepare a warm fallback line for blank moments, such as 'Lovely to see you again, remind me where we last met?'

quiz.question: If someone keeps calling you by the wrong name, what does Post suggest?
options: Correct them sharply the first time
Call them by the wrong name in return
Let it pass at first, then correct them simply if it continues
quiz.explanation: She suggests letting it pass at first, then saying plainly, for example, 'My name is Simpson, not Simpkin.'

cards.title: Don't mistake absent-mindedness for a snub
cards.body:
In Post's day, the 'cut direct', looking straight at someone and refusing to acknowledge them, was a grave insult. But she warns against seeing one where none was meant. People who are preoccupied pass friends without seeing them, and people with bad memories forget even those they liked. That does not excuse the bad memory, she says, but it does explain the seeming rudeness.

Today the same misreading happens with unanswered messages, a colleague who walks past in the corridor, or a friend who forgets your news. Before you decide you've been slighted, consider the boring explanation: they were distracted. Most apparent snubs are nothing of the kind.
cards.quote: On the other hand, one must not confuse absent-mindedness, or a forgetful memory with an intentional 'cut.'
cards.apply_it: Think of a recent moment you felt ignored. Write down one innocent explanation for it before deciding how you feel.

quiz.question: What does Post say about people who pass acquaintances without acknowledging them?
options: Often they are just preoccupied or forgetful, not snubbing anyone
They should be cut in return
quiz.explanation: She warns not to confuse absent-mindedness or forgetfulness with an intentional cut.

cards.title: Conversation should be equal give and take
cards.body:
Post complains that conversation too often becomes all 'take'. The non-stop talker rides a favourite hobby horse for hours, while everyone else waits for a turn that never comes, and laughs loudest at their own long stories. Her cure for the habitual chatterer is short: stop and think.

A useful modern check is to notice the balance. If you have been talking for several minutes, pause and hand the conversation back with a question. If you realise you know far more about your friend's week than they know about yours, that's fine too, but the aim over time is a fair exchange, not a performance with an audience.
cards.quote: Ideal conversation should be a matter of equal give and take, but too often it is all 'take.'
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation, after you finish a story, ask the other person a question about their side before telling another.

quiz.question: What simple rule does Post give the voluble chatterer?
quiz.explanation: Her rule for the chatterer is simply to stop and think.

cards.title: Most conversational blunders come from not thinking about your listener
cards.body:
Post argues that nearly every mistake in conversation comes from not thinking about what you are saying and to whom. Her example is a young mother describing twenty or thirty clever things her baby did to a bachelor seated beside her at dinner. If she had thought for a moment, she would have known that even a dear friend wants only a small taste of that subject.

The point isn't to hide what you love. It's to match the amount to the listener. Your new job, your diet, your fantasy football team or your toddler can all be welcome topics in small portions. Watch the other person's face, and offer a taste rather than the full meal.
cards.quote: Nearly all the faults or mistakes in conversation are caused by not thinking.
cards.apply_it: Before your next social event, pick a topic you love and decide to give it one short story, then ask about the other person.

quiz.question: What does Post say causes nearly all faults in conversation?
quiz.explanation: She says nearly all conversational faults come from not stopping to think about what you say and to whom.

cards.title: The sympathetic listener wins the prize for conversation
cards.body:
After pages of advice to talkers, Post saves her highest praise for the listener. The person who looks glad to see you, seems eager for your news and gives you full, spontaneous attention is the one she would award the prize for the art of conversation.

This is encouraging if you don't think of yourself as witty. You don't need brilliant stories to be good company. Put your phone face down, look at the person, react to what they say and ask the natural follow-up question. People tend to remember how attended to they felt far longer than anything clever you said.
cards.quote: Remember also that the sympathetic (not apathetic) listener is the delight of delights.
cards.locator: =A Few Maxims for Those Who Talk Too Much--and Easily!= ¶5
cards.apply_it: In your next conversation, keep your phone out of sight and ask at least two follow-up questions about something the other person said.

quiz.question: Who does Post say deserves the prize for the art of conversation?
options: The wittiest person in the room
The sympathetic listener who gives undivided attention
The person who knows most facts
quiz.explanation: She gives the palm to the listener who looks glad to see you and gives spontaneous, undivided attention.

cards.title: Small talk is fishing: try topics until one gets a bite
cards.body:
Seated next to a stranger, Post's charming talker behaves like an angler. She offers one topic and gets no nibble, so she tries another, and perhaps a third, until the other person rises to the bait. Post contrasts this with the 'door slammers' who answer every opening with a flat contradiction, such as 'No, hate the theatre', and kill the conversation dead.

This takes the pressure off small talk. You are not expected to find the perfect subject first time. Ask light, open questions about work, travel, books, food or how they know the host, and notice which one makes their face light up. And when someone casts a line to you, give them something to hold on to.
cards.quote: The charming talker is neither more nor less than a fisherman.
cards.apply_it: Prepare three easy opening questions on different subjects to try with the next new person you meet.

quiz.question: What does Post's 'door slammer' do in conversation?
options: Answers with contradiction and flat statement, ending each topic
quiz.explanation: Door slammers meet every topic with contradiction or a flat statement, so no conversation can start.

cards.title: Disagree softly: say 'I don't think I agree', never 'You're wrong'
cards.body:
Post warns against letting a friendly discussion slide into argument. The tactful person keeps prejudices to themselves, and when they do disagree, says something quiet like 'I don't think I agree with you' or 'It seems to me…'. A well-mannered person never barks 'You are wrong!' or 'Nothing of the kind!' If views are utterly opposed, she suggests steering to a pleasanter subject.

This applies to dinner tables and comment sections alike. 'I see it differently' keeps the door open, while 'That's ridiculous' slams it. Not every disagreement must be fought to the end in a social setting. Sometimes the most gracious move is to change the subject.
cards.quote: One who is well-bred never says 'You are wrong!' or 'Nothing of the kind!'
cards.apply_it: Choose a phrase like 'I see it a bit differently' and use it the next time you disagree with someone.

quiz.question: What does Post suggest if someone's opinion is utterly opposed to yours in a social setting?
options: Argue until one of you concedes
quiz.explanation: She says the well-bred person switches to a pleasanter channel of conversation rather than fight it out.

cards.title: Keep ailments and operations out of social conversation
cards.body:
Post's phrase is that you must not take your conversation 'out of the drawing-room'. Operations, illnesses, personal blemishes and bathroom details are neither pleasant nor suitable topics, and neither are jokes at someone's personal expense. Elsewhere she adds that people who are forever telling others about their misfortunes and ailments are rarely invited out.

This isn't about hiding real struggles from people close to you. It's about the setting. A long account of your surgery at a work lunch or a party puts others in an awkward spot. Save the detail for friends who have asked, and keep general company to topics everyone can share.
cards.quote: Operations, ills or personal blemishes, details and appurtenances of the dressing-room, for instance, are neither suitable nor pleasant topics, nor are personal jokes in good taste.
cards.locator: =A Few Important Details of Speech in Conversation= ¶3
cards.apply_it: Notice the next time you're about to describe a health complaint in a group, and ask yourself whether this audience asked for it.

quiz.question: Which topics does Post say to keep out of polite conversation?
quiz.explanation: She lists operations, ills, personal blemishes and dressing-room details as unsuitable topics, along with personal jokes.

cards.title: Speak of others as if they could overhear you
cards.body:
Post offers a resolution for anyone who wants to keep their friends: never speak of someone without imagining that they are listening. She warns that a critical attitude grows like a weed if you let it, and that the boast 'I would say it to her face!' is usually just bravado. Even when it's true, she suggests, think better of it nine times out of ten.

This test works well for group chats, emails and conversations behind closed doors. If the person walked in or saw the screenshot, would you be comfortable? People notice who speaks kindly of the absent, and they trust them more for it.
cards.quote: A very good resolve to make and keep, if you would also keep any friends you make, is never to speak of anyone without, in imagination, having them overhear what you say.
cards.apply_it: Before you send your next message about someone, reread it as if they were the one reading it.

quiz.question: What test does Post suggest before speaking about someone who isn't present?
options: Only say it to close friends
Wait a day before saying it
Imagine they are overhearing what you say
quiz.explanation: Her resolution is never to speak of anyone without imagining them overhearing you.

cards.title: Answer rudeness with a calm, friendly request, not a glare
cards.body:
When people behind you at the theatre won't stop talking, Post says glaring is useless. Young people ignore it, and an angry older person just amuses them. Instead, say amiably: 'I'm sorry, but I can't hear anything while you talk.' If they carry on, ask an usher to fetch the manager. She also reassures readers that most audiences behave well.

The same approach works with loud phone calls on trains, music without headphones or chatter in a cinema. A calm, specific and friendly request gives the other person an easy way to fix it. If it fails, involve the staff whose job it is rather than escalating yourself.
cards.quote: The only thing you can do is to say amiably: 'I'm sorry, but I can't hear anything while you talk.'
cards.apply_it: Write down one calm sentence you could use for a common public annoyance, so it's ready next time.

quiz.question: What does Post advise if people behind you at a performance keep talking?
options: Say amiably that you can't hear, and if needed ask an usher to call the manager
quiz.explanation: She says glaring doesn't work; a friendly remark, then the usher if needed, is the way.

cards.title: Being habitually late is a quiet form of selfishness
cards.body:
Post is blunt: nothing shows a selfish lack of consideration more than being habitually late for dinner. The guests who arrived on time are kept waiting, and the food dries out for everyone. She is especially firm about meals before a play or game, where your lateness makes others miss the start of something they were looking forward to.

Today that covers dinner reservations, meetings, video calls and shared rides. Running late now and then happens; the problem is the habit. Build in a buffer, leave earlier than feels necessary, and if you really will be late, message ahead with an honest time so others can plan.
cards.quote: Nothing shows selfish want of consideration more than being habitually late for dinner.
cards.apply_it: For your next appointment, set your departure alarm ten minutes earlier than you think you need.

quiz.question: Why does Post say lateness before a play is especially bad?
options: It makes others miss the start of the performance
The host has to change the menu
It is bad for your digestion
quiz.explanation: She says it is unfair to make others miss the beginning of a performance through your thoughtless selfishness.

cards.title: Answer invitations promptly, and never drop one for a better offer
cards.body:
Post insists that dinner invitations be answered immediately and that only serious illness, a death or a true emergency excuses breaking one. Accepting one invitation and then cancelling when a grander one arrives marks you, she says, as a snob. Her rule is simple: don't accept an invitation you don't care about. Close friends can agree that plans are provisional, but even then, don't break plans with the same person twice in a short time.

In a world of quick group chats and last-minute cancellations, this is a mark of real respect. Reply soon, say yes only when you mean it, and treat a yes as a promise.
cards.quote: The rule is: 'Don't accept an invitation if you don't care about it.'
cards.apply_it: Reply today to any invitation you've left hanging, with a clear yes or no.

quiz.question: What does Post say about accepting one dinner, then cancelling for a more tempting invitation?
options: It's fine if the new host is more important
It marks you as a snob; decline the first one if you don't care about it
quiz.explanation: She calls it the act of a snob and says not to accept an invitation you don't care about.

cards.title: As a guest, show neither annoyance nor disappointment
cards.body:
Post's standard for guests is famously high. Whatever happens, she says, a guest shows no annoyance or disappointment: you pretend to enjoy the dish you dislike, eat at an hour that doesn't suit you and smile through a picnic in the rain. If a stay is truly unbearable you may find a polite reason to leave, but you never complain to the family, or to anyone else afterwards.

The principle still stands, even if you would raise a real problem like an allergy. Your host has opened their home and effort to you. Small discomforts are part of the price of hospitality, and grumbling, then or later, repays generosity badly.
cards.quote: Courtesy demands that you, when you are a guest, shall show neither annoyance nor disappointment--no matter what happens.
cards.apply_it: On your next visit, find something specific to appreciate and say it, and keep any small gripes to yourself.

quiz.question: According to Post, what should a guest do after a truly uncomfortable stay?
options: Tell the host what went wrong
Not let the family know, nor complain to anyone afterwards
Tell mutual friends how bad it was
quiz.explanation: She says that having broken bread in the house, you must not confide afterwards how wretched you were.

cards.title: Treat your host's home and things better than your own
cards.body:
Post sketches the guest nobody invites twice. They drive the borrowed car hard, leave a borrowed racquet out in the rain, dog-ear the books, burn the table with a cigarette, put wet glasses on polished wood and leave their room looking like a cyclone hit it. She adds those who are late for every meal, invite friends without asking and don't write a thank-you afterwards.

The modern equivalents are easy to picture: the holiday rental left in a mess, the borrowed charger never returned, the friend's sofa you crash on for a week. Respect for other people's property is one of the clearest signs of consideration, and it decides who gets asked back.
cards.quote: The guest no one invites a second time is the one who runs a car to its detriment, and a horse to a lather; who leaves a borrowed tennis racquet out in the rain
cards.apply_it: When you next stay somewhere or borrow something, leave it a little tidier or in better shape than you found it.

quiz.question: Which of these does Post list as behaviour of the guest no one invites again?
options: Inviting their own friends to meals without asking the hostess
Offering to help in the kitchen
quiz.explanation: She names inviting friends to meals without the hostess's permission among the habits that end invitations.

cards.title: A good host makes it look effortless
cards.body:
Post's ideal host puts the guests' comfort first while seeming to make no effort at all. She warns against fussing, fluttering and visible strain, because nothing makes guests more uneasy than feeling they are causing a lot of bother. A good host also keeps annoyances to herself: if the cook quits, the evening becomes a cheerful picnic.

This is reassuring for anyone who hosts in a small flat. Guests don't need perfection; they need to feel welcome and unburdensome. Prepare what you can ahead of time, choose dishes that don't keep you in the kitchen, and when something goes wrong, laugh it off rather than apologising all night.
cards.quote: Nothing makes a guest more uncomfortable than to feel his host or hostess is being put to a great deal of bother or effort on his account.
cards.apply_it: For your next gathering, plan a menu you can mostly prepare before guests arrive, so you can sit with them.

quiz.question: What makes guests most uncomfortable, according to Post?
options: Feeling the host is going to a lot of bother on their account
quiz.explanation: She says nothing makes a guest more uncomfortable than sensing the host is straining on their behalf.

cards.title: Let your guests relax the way they want to
cards.body:
Post's popular hosts strike a balance: some attention, combined with real freedom for guests to spend their time as they like. Her list of hosting don'ts includes interrupting a guest reading on the porch every half page to ask whether they'd rather do something else, and discouraging the guest who wants exercise by predicting rain. She also mocks the anxious host who reads every silence as boredom.

The lesson for weekend visitors and family holidays is to offer options, then step back. Say what's available, check in now and then, and trust adults to know what they enjoy. A quiet guest is often a contented one.
cards.quote: If a guest prefers to sit on the veranda and read, don't interrupt him every half page to ask if he really does not want to do something else.
cards.apply_it: Next time someone stays with you, offer two or three options for the day, then let them choose, including doing nothing.

quiz.question: What does Post's 'anxious hostess' get wrong?
options: She keeps filling her guests' time and assumes silence means boredom
quiz.explanation: The anxious hostess keeps showering suggestions and thinks a silent guest must be bored.

cards.title: Bring the quiet person into the conversation
cards.body:
At a small dinner, Post says, a skilful host acts a little like a showman, bringing each guest forward to the centre of the stage in turn. In a lull she might say to a clever but shy man, 'John, what was that story you told me…' and give him an easy way in on a topic where he shines. She adds that nobody shows to advantage except in a friendly atmosphere.

Anyone can do this, at a team meeting, family dinner or group of friends. Notice who hasn't spoken, remember something they know about, and hand them an opening: 'Priya, you've been to Lisbon, what did you think?' It costs nothing and can transform someone's evening.
cards.quote: She brings each guest forward in turn to the center of the stage.
cards.apply_it: In your next group conversation, invite the quietest person in with a question about something you know they care about.

quiz.question: How does Post's skilful hostess help a shy guest?
options: She asks him to make a speech
She mentions a story he told her so he can take up a topic he shines in
quiz.explanation: She gives the shy guest an easy opening on a subject where he is at his best.

cards.title: Talk to the people seated beside you, even ones you dislike
cards.body:
Post calls it an inflexible rule: at a dinner table you must talk to your neighbours. Even if you are seated next to someone you have quarrelled with, consideration for your host and the rest of the table means you hide your dislike and make at least a show of conversation for a while. She tells of one woman who, rather than chat with a man she despised, recited multiplication tables with him for the hostess's sake.

At weddings, work dinners and family meals, turning your back on a neighbour leaves them stranded and makes the host uneasy. You don't have to become friends. A few courteous minutes is enough.
cards.quote: One inexorable rule of etiquette is that you must talk to your next door neighbor at a dinner table.
cards.apply_it: At your next seated meal, make sure you speak with the people on both sides of you, not just the one you prefer.

quiz.question: Why does Post say you must talk to a dinner neighbour you dislike?
options: Out of consideration for the host and the rest of the table
Because they may be useful later
Because the rules say so, with no reason
quiz.explanation: She says consideration for the hostess and for the table, which is otherwise blocked, requires it.

cards.title: Don't refuse every dish; tell your host about dietary needs in advance
cards.body:
Post notes that refusing dish after dish at someone's table hurts the host, because it suggests you don't like what was cooked. Her advice is to take at least a little and make a show of eating it. If you are on a special diet and said so when you accepted the invitation, she considers it excusable not to eat, though an empty plate all evening still makes you a gloomy companion.

Today, allergies, religious rules and medical diets are common and should be respected. The principle is to tell your host early, so they can plan, and then to eat what you can with appreciation rather than leaving a pointedly empty plate.
cards.quote: If you are 'on a diet' and accepted the invitation with that stipulation, your not eating is excusable
cards.apply_it: When you accept your next invitation, mention any dietary needs right away, and offer to bring a dish if that would help.

quiz.question: When does Post consider not eating at a dinner excusable?
options: When you are on a diet and said so when accepting the invitation
quiz.explanation: She excuses not eating if you are on a diet and stipulated it when you accepted.

cards.title: An awkward thank-you note beats no note at all
cards.body:
After staying in someone's home, Post says a thank-you letter within a few days is absolutely necessary, yet these 'bread and butter letters' are the stumbling-blocks of visitors. Her trick for the stuck writer: draft it as if writing to the friend you actually know, then copy it out to the parent or host. And don't worry that it sounds too informal, because people are pleased by anything that feels friendly and spontaneous.

Her firmest point is that writing nothing is the depth of rudeness, while a clumsy note merely fails to delight. A short message, card or email sent promptly after a visit, meal or gift almost always lands well.
cards.quote: The most awkward note that can be imagined is better than none--for to write none is the depth of rudeness, whereas the awkward note merely fails to delight.
cards.apply_it: Send a three-sentence thank-you today to someone who recently hosted you or gave you something.

quiz.question: What does Post say about a clumsy thank-you note?
options: It should be rewritten until perfect
It is better than none, because writing nothing is the depth of rudeness
quiz.explanation: She says the awkward note merely fails to delight, while writing none is the depth of rudeness.

cards.title: Don't put anger in writing; spoken words fade, written ones stay
cards.body:
Post warns that written words are a poor medium for emotion. The light tone that softens a joke can't be heard on paper, so teasing reads as an accusation. And while angry words spoken aloud fade once the matter is forgiven, anger in a letter becomes, in her phrase, solidified fury, fixed forever.

This is even more true of emails, texts and posts that can be screenshotted and forwarded. If you are upset, talk in person or by phone where your voice can carry nuance, or write the angry draft and don't send it. Save writing for warmth, facts and things you'd be happy to have kept.
cards.quote: Anger in a letter carries with it the effect of solidified fury; the words spoken in reproof melt with the breath of the speaker once the cause is forgiven.
cards.apply_it: Next time you draft an angry message, wait a night before sending, or pick up the phone instead.

quiz.question: Why does Post say anger is worse in a letter than spoken?
options: Written words fix the anger permanently, while spoken words fade once forgiven
quiz.explanation: She says spoken reproof melts once forgiven, but written words fix it for eternity.

cards.title: In a condolence note, simply say what you truly feel
cards.body:
Post says intimate letters of condolence are too personal to follow a set form, and gives only one rule: say what you truly feel, and nothing else. Think of the person you are writing to. Don't dwell on the illness or the manner of death, and don't fill the page with quotations, because tired, grieving eyes can't follow long passages. Write simply and briefly, as if your note were a handclasp.

If you've been putting off a sympathy message because you can't find the right words, this may help. There are no right words. A few honest lines, such as 'I'm so sorry. I'm thinking of you', are enough, and they mean more than eloquence.
cards.quote: One rule, and one only, should guide you in writing such letters. Say what you truly feel. Say that and nothing else.
cards.apply_it: If there's someone grieving you haven't contacted, write them two honest sentences today. They don't need to be perfect.

quiz.question: What does Post advise avoiding in a condolence letter?
options: Dwelling on the details of illness or death, and long quotations
quiz.explanation: She advises against dwelling on illness or the manner of death and quoting endlessly from poets and Scripture.

cards.title: Share one small memory of the person who died
cards.body:
Post writes that a condolence letter may be abrupt, badly built or ungrammatical, and it doesn't matter. Grace of expression counts for nothing; sincerity is everything. What comforts most is some personal note about the one who was loved and will be missed. She gives the example of a soldier writing of a friend: 'Poor old Steve, what a peach he was!' And she suggests asking whether there is anything you can do for the family.

A small story, such as how they laughed or a kindness they once did you, may seem trivial now. But she imagines each such letter as a single sprig, and many together planting a whole garden of memory for the family.
cards.quote: your letter and that of many others, each bringing a single sprig, may plant a whole memory-garden in the hearts of the bereaved.
cards.apply_it: If you write to a grieving family, include one specific memory of the person, however small.

quiz.question: What does Post say matters most in a letter of condolence?
options: Sincerity and a personal note about the one who is missed
quiz.explanation: She says grace of expression counts for nothing and sincerity alone is of value.

cards.title: Supporting the bereaved means forgetting yourself and offering practical help
cards.body:
Post writes with real tenderness about people in fresh grief. Shock unsettles body and mind; mourners may be cold, sleepless and unable to face even people they love. Nobody should be pressed on them, and no friend has a right to feel hurt if they are told they can't be received. Some people find company a comfort, while others shrink from it.

If you are the one helping, she says, put aside all thought of yourself, like a good nurse, because service is the only gift of value. In practice that may mean dropping off food, handling a phone call or an errand, and accepting a 'not now' graciously.
cards.quote: service is the only gift of value that can be offered.
cards.apply_it: If someone you know is grieving, offer one specific practical task, such as a meal or an errand, rather than 'let me know if you need anything'.

quiz.question: What does Post say about friends who are told they can't be received by a grieving family?
options: They should stop contacting the family
They have no right to feel hurt
They should send a long letter instead
quiz.explanation: She says none have the right to feel hurt if told they can be of no use or cannot be received.

cards.title: At work, good manners are consideration for everyone's interests
cards.body:
Post argues that etiquette matters in business more than people think, and she defines it in practical terms: good manners are nothing more than courteous consideration of other people's interests and feelings. A manager who says good morning to staff and treats everyone with respect, she says, earns their regard rather than just flattering them.

It follows, she asks, that customers, bosses and employees all prefer someone whose manners show they are considering the customer's, the company's and the staff's interests as well as their own. That is a fair description of a trustworthy colleague or leader today.
cards.quote: good manners are, after all, nothing but courteous consideration of other people's interests and feelings.
cards.apply_it: At work this week, greet each person on your team by name at least once and ask how something of theirs is going.

quiz.question: How does Post define good manners in a business setting?
options: Courteous consideration of other people's interests and feelings
quiz.explanation: She says good manners are nothing but courteous consideration of other people's interests and feelings.

cards.title: When someone is speaking to you, give them your full attention
cards.body:
Post describes a company president whose charm lies in making every visitor feel their business is the most important thing in his day, because whenever he sees someone, he gives them undivided attention. By contrast, the man who stares out of the window, doodles on his blotter or inspects his fingernails while someone talks may think he is being clever, or is simply bored.

Either way, she says, he loses. Plenty of people are bored, but those who show it are always at fault. In meetings and calls today the doodling is often a phone or a second screen. Closing the laptop and looking at the speaker is a simple form of respect people notice.
cards.quote: To listen attentively when one is spoken to, is merely one of the rules of etiquette.
cards.apply_it: In your next meeting, close other tabs and put your phone away while each person speaks.

quiz.question: What does Post say about people who show boredom while others are speaking?
options: It's fine if the topic is dull
They are always at fault for showing it
It helps end the meeting sooner
quiz.explanation: She says lots of people are bored, often by their own fault, but those who show it are always at fault.

cards.title: Earn the right to correct people by knowing the work
cards.body:
Post tells of a company officer in a good suit who scolds a machinist at his lathe for poor work. The worker resents it: who is this man to teach him his job? Now imagine, she says, that the officer took off his coat and ran the lathe himself with real skill. From then on, the worker and everyone watching would listen to him with respect.

Her point is that authority comes from knowledge, not position. Whenever you know as much as someone else about a subject, you are their equal on it, whatever your rank. For managers today, criticism lands better when you clearly understand the work, and is best paired with showing how.
cards.quote: Whenever you know as much as the other man, whether you are socially above, or below him, you are on that subject his equal; when you know more than he does, you have the advantage.
cards.apply_it: Before giving feedback on someone's work this week, spend ten minutes understanding how that task is actually done.

quiz.question: In Post's lathe story, what would have won the worker's respect?
options: The officer showing he could do the job expertly himself
quiz.explanation: She says that if the officer had operated the lathe skilfully, the worker would have listened without resentment.

cards.title: Your manners at home are the real test
cards.body:
Post begins her chapter on everyday home life with a simple image: no chain is stronger than its weakest link, and no manners will stand a strain beyond what they are tested with daily at home. People who lose their temper with their family, she says, will sooner or later lose it in public. A family without courtesy at home can't convincingly put it on for visitors.

It is easy to save our patience for colleagues and strangers and give our loved ones what's left. But the people we live with deserve the best of our manners, not the leftovers, and the habits we practise at home are the ones that show up everywhere else.
cards.quote: Those who are used to losing their temper in the bosom of their family will sooner or later lose it in public.
cards.locator: Chapter XXXVI. Every-day Manners at Home ¶2
cards.apply_it: Today, say please and thank you to the people you live with as carefully as you would to a colleague.

quiz.question: What does Post predict about people who often lose their temper at home?
options: They will be calmer in public
They will sooner or later lose it in public too
quiz.explanation: She says those used to losing their temper with family will sooner or later lose it in public.

cards.title: Children follow what you do, not what you preach
cards.body:
Post insists that a parent's daily example outweighs any preacher. If children see temper uncontrolled, hear gossip and suspicion of neighbours, or watch sharp dealing, their own characters can hardly escape. And no child, she says, will accept a rule that the person preaching it doesn't follow. It is a waste of breath to tell children to keep their temper or play fair if you don't.

This is humbling and hopeful at once. You don't need perfect lectures; you need to model the behaviour you want, including apologising when you get it wrong. Children learn courtesy by watching how you treat them, your partner, the neighbours and the person at the till.
cards.quote: No child will ever accept a maxim that is preached but not followed by the preacher.
cards.locator: Chapter XXXVI. Every-day Manners at Home ¶7
cards.apply_it: Pick one habit you nag your children about and check this week whether you model it yourself.

quiz.question: According to Post, what is the greatest influence on children's manners?
options: The daily example of their parents
quiz.explanation: She says no preacher can equal the influence of admirable parents' daily example.

cards.title: Don't let persistent nagging turn your 'no' into a 'yes'
cards.body:
In her chapter on children's manners, Post says that once a child has been told 'no', they must never be allowed to win a 'yes' through persistent nagging. She sees well-behaved children as the result of patient, consistent training, and badly behaved ones as victims of parents who were too negligent to provide it. She also notes that such children often grow up to blame the parents who spoiled them.

Much of her approach to discipline is of its time, but this point is still widely shared. If pestering works, children learn to pester. Decide carefully before you answer, then stay calm and consistent, so 'no' means no.
cards.quote: after having been told 'no,' they must never be allowed by persistent nagging to win 'yes.'
cards.apply_it: Before answering your child's next request, take a moment to decide, then hold to your answer kindly if they push.

quiz.question: What happens, by Post's logic, when nagging turns a parent's 'no' into a 'yes'?
options: The child learns that nagging works
quiz.explanation: If persistent nagging wins, the child learns to keep nagging; she says it must never be allowed to.

cards.title: Treat children like guests at the table and they'll learn to behave like guests
cards.body:
Post observes that children are natural imitators. When a parent eats alone with them, she suggests letting them talk freely while quietly training them in table conversation as well as table manners. If the parent treats them exactly as they would treat visitors, the children play 'visitor' to perfection. She adds that nothing hurts children more than not being allowed to act grown-up once they can, such as cutting their own food.

Family meals remain one of the best places to practise. Ask children real questions, listen to the answers, pass dishes politely, and let them do what they can for themselves. Manners caught this way tend to stick.
cards.quote: If their mother treats them exactly as she does her visitors they in turn play 'visitor' to perfection.
cards.apply_it: At your next family meal, ask each child one real question and listen to the answer as you would to an adult guest.

quiz.question: What does Post say hurts children's feelings at table?
options: Not being allowed to behave like grown persons when they feel able
quiz.explanation: She says being fed and having food cut up after they can manage it holds back their development and hurts their feelings.

cards.title: Plan activities for children on long journeys instead of just saying 'be good'
cards.body:
Post points out that it is unreasonable to expect small children to sit quietly for hours just because they've been told to be good. She admired a pair of little girls on a train who were crocheting doll sweaters from balls of wool with small prizes wound inside. When they reached a prize, they played with it for a while, then went back to crocheting.

The idea of pacing out small surprises still works on flights and road trips. Pack a few wrapped treats, books or activities to bring out at intervals. It keeps children occupied and spares fellow travellers, which Post also cared about.
cards.quote: it is unreasonable to expect little children to sit quietly for hours on end by merely telling them to 'be good.'
cards.apply_it: Before your next trip with children, pack three small wrapped surprises to hand out at set points in the journey.

quiz.question: How did the girls in Post's example stay occupied on the train?
options: Crocheting with balls of wool that had small prizes wound inside
quiz.explanation: They crocheted doll sweaters from wool that hid prizes, earning each one as the wool ran out.

cards.title: Don't spend your partner's sympathy on small complaints
cards.body:
Post warns couples against saving up every petty trouble to pour onto the person they love most. If every greeting is met with a new grievance, the partner can only say 'I'm so sorry, dear' again and again. She uses a striking image: there is a big deposit of sympathy in the bank of love, but if you keep drawing out little sums, it may be gone when you really need it. She applies the same advice to husbands, who shouldn't unload every irritation of the working day either.

Real problems, she says, are different. The point is to share the serious things and let the trivial ones go.
cards.quote: There is a big deposit of sympathy in the bank of love, but don't draw out little sums every hour or so
cards.apply_it: Tonight, greet your partner with something good from your day before mentioning any minor annoyance.

quiz.question: What does Post's 'bank of love' image warn against?
options: Spending too much money on gifts
Drawing on a partner's sympathy for every petty complaint
quiz.explanation: She warns that small, constant withdrawals of sympathy can leave nothing when you truly need it.

cards.title: Let your friends get to know a new partner, then decide with eyes open
cards.body:
Post admired the way young people of the 1920s socialised in groups. When a stranger began courting a young woman, her friends watched him with one question: is he good enough for her? If they liked him, he joined the group. If they didn't, they told her frankly. And if she still chose to marry him, she at least decided with her eyes open.

Our friends often see what infatuation hides. Introducing a new partner to the people who know you best, and really listening to their impressions, is still wise. The choice is yours, but it's better made knowing what clear-sighted friends think.
cards.quote: If she is really in love with him and determined to marry in spite of their frankly given opinion, she at least makes her decision with her eyes open.
cards.apply_it: If you're dating someone new, ask one trusted friend for their honest impression, and listen without defending.

quiz.question: What question did the friends in Post's group ask about a newcomer?
options: Is he good enough for Mary?
Is he from a good family?
quiz.explanation: The group's protective question was, 'Is he good enough for Mary?'

cards.title: Plan a wedding you can afford, because simple can be beautiful
cards.body:
Post is clear that a wedding should match the family's means. Spending beyond what you can afford is unwise, she says, and inappropriate lavishness invites more criticism than modesty, which needn't lack charm. She describes a poor bride marrying in June in a village church decorated with dogwood by her sisters and neighbours, in a dress she made herself, with a homemade cake and a borrowed record player for music.

Guests remembered that wedding as one of the loveliest they'd seen. With modern weddings often costing a fortune, her point stands. What people remember is the couple's happiness and the warmth of the day, not the price tag.
cards.quote: It is not only inadvisable for them to attempt expenditure beyond what they can afford, but they would lay themselves open to far greater criticism through inappropriate lavishness, than through meagerness of arrangement
cards.locator: =Breach of Etiquette for Groom to Give Wedding= ¶2
cards.apply_it: If you're planning a celebration, set the budget first, then list the three details that matter most to you.

quiz.question: What does Post say about a lavish wedding beyond the family's means?
options: It invites more criticism than a simple one
It is expected of every family
quiz.explanation: She says inappropriate lavishness invites far greater criticism than modest arrangements.

cards.title: At a wedding, keep the conversation on the couple and keep it brief
cards.body:
Post gives many examples of what to say to newlyweds in a receiving line, but stresses there is no script, just one rule. Don't launch into long talk about yourself: how you feel, what happened to you, or what you wore at your own wedding. The subject should stay with the couple, their wedding and their future. Be brief so the people behind you aren't kept waiting. She also says it's poor manners to congratulate a bride on having secured a husband.

The same applies to graduations, birthdays and promotions. A warm, specific line about them, then step aside so others get their turn.
cards.quote: Your subject must not deviate from the young couple themselves, their wedding, their future.
cards.apply_it: At the next celebration you attend, prepare one warm sentence about the person being celebrated, and keep yourself out of it.

quiz.question: What does Post say you should avoid in a wedding receiving line?
quiz.explanation: She says not to launch into details of yourself; keep the subject on the couple and be brief.

cards.title: Remember your partner's parents on the big day
cards.body:
Post singles out one thing a bride must not forget at the end of the wedding: to send for her husband's parents and say goodbye to them before leaving. In the rush, she says, a couple can easily dash past without a glance, and many a mother has gone home with an ache in her heart. The groom's parents may be shy, in an unfamiliar house, and waiting to be asked.

It's a small act with a large effect, and it reaches beyond weddings. At any family event, the in-laws or newcomers who know fewer people can feel like outsiders. Go and find them, include them, and say a proper goodbye.
cards.quote: many a mother seeing her son and new daughter rush past without even a glance from either of them, has returned home with an ache in her heart.
cards.locator: =Bride's First Duty of Thought for Groom's Parents= ¶2
cards.apply_it: At your next family gathering, seek out your partner's relatives and spend a few minutes with them before you leave.

quiz.question: Why might the groom's parents not come to say goodbye on their own, according to Post?
options: They may be shy in an unknown house and waiting to be invited
It's against custom for them to do so
quiz.explanation: She says they may be strangers and shy, hesitating in an unknown house until invited.

cards.title: Be a cheerful loser and a quiet winner
cards.body:
Post's rules for sport are short: never lose your temper, play for the sake of playing rather than to win, don't suddenly complain of an injury when you're losing, and always give your opponent the benefit of the doubt, even if it costs you the point. Her summary is that a true sportsman is a cheerful loser and a quiet winner, who openly admires others' strengths and works on their own weaknesses.

That fits office competitions, family board games and children's football alike. Gloating and sulking both make others regret playing with you. How you handle a result says more about you than the score does.
cards.quote: A true sportsman is always a cheerful loser, a quiet winner, with a very frank appreciation of the admirable traits in others, which he seeks to emulate, and his own shortcomings, which he tries to improve.
cards.apply_it: Next time you lose a game, congratulate the winner with one specific thing they did well.

quiz.question: Which of these is one of Post's rules of sportsmanship?
options: Give your opponent the benefit of the doubt
Point out the other side's mistakes
quiz.explanation: She says always give the opponent the benefit of the doubt, even if it costs you the point.

cards.title: Credit your partner's good moves instead of blaming the result
cards.body:
Writing about bridge partners, Post describes the ideal one: they never criticise your mistakes, notice your good decisions, and give you credit whether the hand was won or lost. The poor partner judges you only by the result and blames you when things go wrong, even if the loss was their fault. She adds a sharp psychological point: constant fault-finding makes you play your worst, while appreciation acts like a tonic.

This holds for work partners, co-parents, team-mates and couples. Notice good effort, not just good outcomes, and hold back the instant post-mortem. People perform better around someone who believes in them.
cards.quote: Also, to be continually found fault with makes you play your worst; whereas appreciation of good judgment on your part acts as a tonic and you play seemingly 'better than you know how.'
cards.apply_it: Today, point out one good decision a partner or colleague made, regardless of how it turned out.

quiz.question: What effect does Post say constant fault-finding has on a partner?
options: It makes them play their worst
It makes them try harder and win
quiz.explanation: She says being continually found fault with makes you play your worst, while appreciation acts as a tonic.

cards.title: Don't give advice nobody asked for
cards.body:
In the middle of her notes on golf, Post states a rule she says applies to bridge and every other game: don't appoint yourself someone's coach. Unless your advice is asked for, don't tell others how to hold their clubs, which ones to use or how to play the shot.

It's a rule worth carrying well beyond the golf course. Unasked-for tips on someone's parenting, diet, driving, career or cooking usually land as criticism, however kindly meant. If you think you can help, ask first: 'Would you like a suggestion?' If they say no, let it go.
cards.quote: Unless your advice is asked for, you should not instruct others how to hold their clubs or which ones to use, or how they ought to make the shot.
cards.apply_it: Next time you're tempted to offer a tip, ask 'Would you like a suggestion?' first, and accept a no.

quiz.question: What rule does Post apply to golf, bridge and every other game?
options: Don't appoint yourself mentor unless your advice is asked for
quiz.explanation: She says not to instruct others unless your advice is asked for.

cards.title: Dress to suit the occasion, and when in doubt, go plainer
cards.body:
Post knew fashions would change too fast to pin down, so she offered one unchanging principle: suitability. That means clothes that suit your age and the event, and also clothes in proportion to your income and surroundings. Her safest rule: when in doubt, wear the plainer outfit, since it's far better to be underdressed than overdressed. She also mocked people who copy every trend whether it suits them or not.

Dressing with care is a way of showing respect for your host and the occasion, not a matter of vanity. Choose what fits the setting and your budget, and you'll rarely go wrong.
cards.quote: There is one rule that is fairly safe to follow: When in doubt, wear the plainer dress. It is always better far to be under-dressed than over-dressed.
cards.apply_it: Before your next event, check the dress code or ask the host, and if still unsure, choose the simpler option.

quiz.question: What one unchanging principle of dress does Post give?
options: Spend as much as you can
Suitability, including to your income and surroundings
quiz.explanation: She names suitability, meaning suitable to age, occasion, income and surroundings.

cards.title: Traveling together shows who you really are
cards.body:
Post's perfect traveller is cheerful, punctual, packed on time, unbothered by discomfort and blessed with a sense of humour. She warns that you can't always have good weather, perfect connections or everything to your liking, and that refusing to be philosophical just makes things worse for you and everyone else. If you hate long walks, don't start one and then expect the group to turn back.

She calls travel the greatest test of a person's wearing qualities. The friend who stays good-humoured through delays and wrong turns is the one who gets asked on the next trip.
cards.quote: There is no greater test of a man's (or a woman's) 'wearing' qualities than traveling with him.
cards.apply_it: On your next trip, when something goes wrong, be the first to find something funny or good about it.

quiz.question: Which quality does Post include in her perfect traveller?
options: Punctuality and being packed on time
quiz.explanation: She lists punctuality, with bags packed and down at the hour of starting, among the perfect traveller's virtues.

cards.title: If a friendly approach isn't returned, let it go
cards.body:
Post writes about the over-eager passenger who tracks down possible acquaintances on a ship and insists on chatting to the person in the next deck chair. A few remarks to an idle neighbour are fine, and a warm response invites more. But a reply in single words means they would rather be left alone, and nobody should interrupt someone reading or writing.

Her one rule: any approach should be tentative, and if it isn't met halfway, withdraw it at once. People who want solitude have as much right to it as sociable people have to company. That's a good guide for seatmates on planes, new neighbours and the office kitchen.
cards.quote: Whoever is making the advance, whether your neighbor or yourself, it must never be more than tentative; if not at least met halfway, it must be withdrawn at once.
cards.apply_it: Next time you chat to a stranger, watch for short answers or a book or headphones, and take the hint gracefully.

quiz.question: What should you do if a friendly approach to a stranger is answered in monosyllables?
options: Take it to mean they prefer to be left alone
Keep trying until they warm up
quiz.explanation: She says monosyllabic answers mean they prefer their own diversions, and an unreturned advance should be withdrawn.
